3    Q.   What is the general process SPS uses to establish its New Mexico retail revenue

4         requirement?

5    A.   At a very general level, setting utility rates is a three-step process. The first step

 6        involves a revenue requirement study, which is sometimes referred to as a cost-of-

 7        service study or pro forma rate of return study. The second step involves the

 8        allocation of costs among the jurisdictions that the utility serves. I will discuss each

 9        of those steps in more detail in the remainder of this section of my testimony. The

10        third step entails the separation of the costs for the New Mexico retail jurisdiction

11        into various functions (e.g., production, transmission, distribution). SPS witness

12        Taylor J. Hurt discusses the allocation of costs between the various jurisdictions

13        and functions, as well as presents the class cost of service study, which allocates

14        the New Mexico retail jurisdictional revenue requirement amongst SPS’s New

15        Mexico retail customer classes. SPS witness Alexander G. Trowbridge discusses

16        the proposed rate design to recover those amounts by customer class based upon

17        test year billing determinants. Lastly, Mr. Trowbridge describes the link between

18        the proposed rate design and the class cost of service study presented by Mr. Hurt.

 1   A.   Development of the Overall Revenue Requirement

 2   Q.   What is a revenue requirement study?

 3   A.   A revenue requirement study is a model that examines all company investments,

 4        revenues, and expenses associated with providing electric utility service over a

 5        specific 12-month period, with the goal of determining the company’s cost of

 6        providing service to its customers. The revenue requirement study establishes the

 7        total revenue needed for the company to earn its authorized return, which is used in

 8        setting the company’s base rates for service. In effect, the revenue requirement

 9        establishes what the utility’s cost of service will be in future periods when the new

10        rates will be in effect.

11   Q.   Please describe the test year that SPS utilized for purposes of this case.

12   A.   Pursuant to Commission Rule 17.1.3.1 et seq. (the “Future Test Year Period

13        Rule”),8 SPS is using a future test year in this rate case based on the period

14        December 1, 2026, through November 30, 2027 (the “Future Test Year”). A future

15        test year period as defined by the rule means a 12-month period beginning no later

16        than the date the proposed rate change is expected to take effect.9

 1   Q.       What is the starting point for a revenue requirement study?

 2   A.       The starting point in developing SPS’s revenue requirement study is total company

 3            per-book accounting information for a given base period. The Base Period used for

 4            this proceeding is the 12-month period from July 1, 2024, through June 30, 2025.

 5            To tie to the financial statements’ per-book values, SPS must make several manual

 6            adjustments referred to as “Base Data” adjustments for information that is not

 7            automatically integrated from the general ledger system into the Regulatory

 8            Information System (“RIS”) discussed in the next section. A complete list of “Base

 9            Data” adjustments can be found in Attachment AMJ-14.

10   Q.       Does this starting point change when utilizing a future test year?

11   A.       No. The starting point remains the same. There are, however, a few additional steps

12            to determine the amounts requested in the Future Test Year as compared to a

13            historical test year. As with a historical test year, SPS adjusts per-book data to arrive

14            at the Adjusted Base Period.10

 9   Q.   What types of adjustments are made to the per-book accounting data to

10        develop the Adjusted Base Period?

11   A.   Three types of adjustments are typically made to the per-book data to arrive at the

12        Adjusted Base Period amount: (1) accounting adjustments; (2) Commission-

13        required adjustments; and (3) pro forma adjustments. A complete list of “Base

14        Period Adjustments” can be found in Attachment AMJ-14.

15   Q.   What are accounting adjustments?

16   A.   Accounting adjustments include both out-of-period adjustments and adjustments to

17        eliminate or add certain accounts, expenses, or revenues. Out-of-period adjustments

 1        eliminate transactions that were recorded in the Base Period but apply to periods

 5        Base Period, Linkage Data, or the Future Test Year are added, and thus reflected in

 8   Q.   The second type of adjustment you mentioned is a “Commission-required

 9        adjustment.” What is that?

10   A.   Commission-required adjustments are made to comply with rate recovery policies

11        and principles established by the Commission in its rules and in orders issued in

12        prior proceedings. For example, promotional and image advertising expenses are

13        costs the Commission has specifically required to be eliminated from the cost of

14        service, as are costs incurred for political purposes. In isolating the effects on the

15        cost of service for New Mexico, when these expenses are excluded, so are the tax

16        deductions associated with them.

17   Q.   The third type of adjustment is a “pro forma adjustment.” What is that?

18   A.   Pro forma adjustments are made to the Base Period per-book results so that the

19        Future Test Year will be representative of conditions during the period when the

 2   Q.   Please turn to the second step in the ratemaking process—jurisdictional

 3        allocation. Why is it necessary to perform a jurisdictional allocation?

 4   A.   Well-established principles of cost causation require that customers in a particular

 5        jurisdiction pay only the costs associated with providing service to that jurisdiction.

 6        Thus, in this case, the revenue requirement ultimately determined for New Mexico

 7        retail customers should include only costs related to the provision of retail utility

 8        service in New Mexico. The process to allocate costs among utility jurisdictions

 9        creates a stand-alone financial look at the revenue requirement for the cost of

10        serving SPS’s New Mexico retail jurisdiction, which is then compared to the pro

11        forma present revenues to determine any deficiency or excess. Any excess would

12        indicate SPS is earning more than its costs of service, whereas a deficiency

13        indicates SPS is not, or would not, in the context of a future test year, recover the

14        cost of providing service to its customers and, thus, a rate increase is warranted.
